messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  (none)

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rafael Mendez, a 58-year-old forensic analyst, had spent most of his adult life believing that careful observation and procedure could make sense of chaos. That assumption was shattered on a weekday afternoon when a man-made disaster struck the municipal records building where he was working. Rafael had been in a lower-floor evidence room when the blast hit, hard enough to send a wave of heat and debris through the corridor and buckle the lights overhead. In the immediate confusion he heard alarms, cracking concrete, and people shouting names from the stairwell while smoke began seeping under the door. He escaped with others through a side exit, but the image that stayed with him was of a workplace he knew intimately turned into a place he could not read or control in a matter of seconds. In the months that followed, what unsettled him most was not only the memory of the explosion itself but the way ordinary spaces suddenly felt unknowable. He began avoiding unfamiliar places whenever he could, telling his wife that if he did not already know the exits, the crowds, and the layout, he could not assess the danger. A new restaurant, a different route to the grocery store, even an unfamiliar parking garage could make him tense up before he stepped inside, as though his body were bracing for another sudden rupture.

At work, the consequences of that changed way of moving through the world became harder to hide. Rafael still came in, but he took the same route, parked in the same spot, and resisted assignments that required him to visit new sites unless there was no one else available. The municipal building had once been a place where his expertise felt reliable; now, when he walked into an unfamiliar evidence storage facility or a temporary office set up after a fire inspection, he felt his attention narrow immediately to the exits, the windows, the noise in the hall. He described being jumpy, easily startled by a printer slamming shut or a coworker appearing at his elbow. His body, he said, never fully settled anymore. Even at home in the quiet of the evening, he noticed a constant tension through his shoulders and jaw, as if some part of him remained on duty for danger that might arrive without warning. This left him exhausted and irritated, and it fed his growing conviction that his reactions since the disaster showed he was a lousy coper. He had built an identity around being the man who stayed calm when others panicked, the one who could sort evidence, follow the facts, and remain steady under pressure. Now he felt that those traits belonged to someone he used to be. He was no longer sure he could do the things that had defined him for decades, and that loss struck him as humiliating as well as frightening.

Rafael’s view of the world had become darker in the same period. He had come to believe that the world is a dangerous place, and he found himself thinking that danger could appear anywhere people gathered, especially in unfamiliar settings where he could not quickly judge what might go wrong. That belief made him even more determined to keep to predictable routines, which narrowed his life in ways his wife noticed before he admitted them himself. He stopped joining her when she wanted to try new neighborhood places and declined an invitation from relatives to meet at a restaurant across town. The avoidance brought short-term relief, but it also left him feeling increasingly cut off from ordinary life and from the part of himself that used to move through the city with confidence. When he had to cross an unfamiliar lobby or enter a new office building for work, he found himself scanning every corner, as if vigilance alone might prevent another disaster. Over time, the strain showed in his posture and in the way he hesitated before agreeing to simple changes in routine.

What finally brought Rafael to seek help was the recognition that the narrowing of his life was no longer something he could explain away as caution. He had been awakened the previous week by a sudden clang from a neighbor’s remodeling work and found himself sitting upright, heart racing, unable to settle for nearly an hour. His wife told him he was becoming unreachable, always on edge, always checking, always saying no. Rafael came to treatment not because he believed the disaster was over, but because he feared he was being transformed by it into someone permanently guarded and diminished. More than anything, he wanted to recover a sense that he could move through the world without feeling constantly threatened, and he feared that if nothing changed, the man he once was would remain out of reach.
